title: Seconds Until One Buyer Is Done
statement:
People stand in a line at a ticket window. Person i (0-indexed from the front) wants tickets[i] tickets.

Each second, the person at the front buys exactly one ticket. If they still need more, they go to the back of the line; otherwise they leave.

Return the number of seconds until the person who started at position k has all of their tickets.

examples.why: Order of purchases: 0, 1, 2, 0, 2. Person 2 finishes on the 5th second; person 0 still needs one more.
Before person 1's final purchase, everyone ahead of them buys twice and everyone behind buys only once (person 3 needs just 1). 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 6.
The first person needs one ticket and is served first.

hints: You could simulate the line second by second. But how many tickets does each other person buy before person k is done?
Person k buys tickets[k] times. Someone standing ahead of k gets one more turn than k in every round up to and including the last one.
Ahead of or at k: they buy min(tickets[i], tickets[k]). Behind k: they buy min(tickets[i], tickets[k] − 1), because the line stops the moment k finishes.

explain.intuition:
Each second is one purchase, so the answer is the number of purchases made up to k's last one. Think in rounds: in each full round everyone still in line buys once. Person k is done after round tickets[k].

People in front of k get their turn in that last round before k does, so they buy up to tickets[k] tickets. People behind k never get the last round, so they buy at most tickets[k] − 1. Anyone who needs fewer simply leaves early.
pitfalls: Using min(tickets[i], t) for everyone. People behind k lose the final round, as in the second example.
Simulating with an array shift per second is fine here, but it is O(n) per step in JavaScript and hides the counting idea.

solutions.title: Simulate rounds
solutions.idea: Walk the line in rounds, decrementing each person with tickets left, until person k reaches zero.

solutions.title: Count each person's purchases
solutions.idea: People up to k buy min(tickets[i], t); people after k buy min(tickets[i], t − 1).

followups: Answer the question for every person at once. Can you do better than n separate O(n) passes?
Each person may buy up to two tickets per turn. How does the formula change?
